root.stem: A 47-year-old African American man comes in because a dark spot on the sole of his left foot has grown over 3 years. It began as a flat brown mole he has had since childhood and is now asymmetric and partly raised, about 9 mm across, with a notched border and patches of brown, black and blue-gray. He sails every weekend without sunscreen and says he never burns; the skin of his face, forearms and back shows no lesions. He has no enlarged lymph nodes. A biopsy shows atypical cells packed with dense brown pigment granules that extend into the dermis.
root.oneliner: 47M + African American + sails weekly without sunscreen, never burns, sun-exposed skin clear + childhood mole on the sole grown over 3 years + asymmetric, partly raised 9 mm lesion + notched border + brown, black and blue-gray + atypical cells with dense brown pigment granules extending into the dermis
highlight: mole he has had since childhood
asymmetric and partly raised, about 9 mm across
patches of brown, black and blue-gray
skin of his face, forearms and back shows no lesions

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A cancer of pigment-making cells (melanocytes). The clincher: **a changing mole that is asymmetric, with a notched border, several colors and a width over 6 mm, and a biopsy of atypical cells packed with melanin granules**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same cancer; exam options often use this one.

nodes.q: Which rule of thumb flags a mole as suspicious?
nodes.a: ABCDE: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolving
nodes.note: He has all five. **Evolving (a mole that grows or changes over time)** is the single most important warning sign.

nodes.q: From which embryonic tissue do the cancer cells come?
nodes.note: Melanocytes migrate from the neural crest to the basal layer of the epidermis.

nodes.q: Which subtype of melanoma is a pigmented lesion on the sole of a Black patient?
nodes.note: The most common melanoma subtype in darker-skinned people. It arises on the **palms, soles and under the nails**, so these are the sites to examine in a Black patient, and it is not caused by sunlight. In fair skin the most common subtype is superficial spreading melanoma, often on the back in men and the legs in women.

nodes.q: His sun-exposed skin is clear despite weekly sailing without sunscreen. What protects it?
nodes.a: More melanin, in larger melanosomes that are passed to keratinocytes; the number of melanocytes is the same as in fair skin
nodes.note: Skin color depends on melanin content and melanosome size, not on how many melanocytes there are. This is why sun-related melanoma, basal cell carcinoma and actinic keratosis are uncommon in dark skin.

nodes.q: His cancer grew out of his childhood mole. What was that mole called on biopsy before it changed?
nodes.note: About a third of melanomas arise in a pre-existing nevus; the rest arise in normal skin. Freckles, seborrheic keratosis, actinic keratosis and acanthosis nigricans are not precursors of melanoma.

nodes.q: Which immunostains confirm that the atypical pigmented cells are melanocytes?
nodes.a: S-100 and HMB-45 (also Melan-A and SOX10)
nodes.note: The brown-black pigment is melanin. S-100 is also positive in Schwann cells and Langerhans cells, so HMB-45 or Melan-A adds specificity.

nodes.q: Which biopsy measurement sets the prognosis?
nodes.a: Breslow thickness (depth of invasion in millimetres)
nodes.note: Deeper tumors reach lymphatics and blood vessels. Thickness also sets the surgical margin and the need for a node biopsy.

nodes.q: Invasion into which layer of the skin carries the worst outlook?
nodes.a: The deepest layer reached, the subcutaneous tissue
nodes.note: Outlook worsens step by step: epidermis, papillary dermis, reticular dermis, subcutaneous tissue. Tumor confined above the basement membrane (in situ) is cured by excision; once cells enter the dermis they reach lymphatics.

nodes.q: Where does it spread first?
nodes.a: Regional lymph nodes (for his foot, the groin nodes)
nodes.note: Then lung, liver, brain and bone. Melanoma is a classic cause of brain metastases.

nodes.q: Which procedure checks the first draining node?
nodes.note: Discussed for tumors about 0.8 mm or thicker (or thinner but ulcerated). Node status is the strongest predictor after thickness.

nodes.q: What is the treatment of the primary lesion?
nodes.a: Wide local excision, with margin width set by Breslow thickness
nodes.note: Roughly 0.5 to 1 cm for in situ disease, 1 cm for tumors up to 1 mm, 1 to 2 cm for 1 to 2 mm, and 2 cm beyond that. Diagnose by excisional biopsy with narrow margins; never shave a suspicious pigmented lesion.

nodes.q: Which gene is mutated in about half of melanomas and is a drug target?
nodes.note: The mutant kinase is permanently active and drives the MAPK growth-signalling pathway. BRAF mutations are common in melanoma of intermittently sun-exposed skin; acral melanoma like his carries them less often and more often has KIT mutations, so the tumor is tested before targeted drugs are chosen.

nodes.q: Which drug class blocks the mutant kinase?
nodes.a: BRAF inhibitors, such as vemurafenib or dabrafenib
nodes.note: Used for advanced disease, often with a MEK inhibitor to delay resistance.

nodes.q: Which drug class works in advanced disease whatever the mutation?
nodes.a: Immune checkpoint inhibitors: anti-programmed death-1 antibodies (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) and anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab)
nodes.note: They release the brake on T cells that recognise the tumor.

nodes.q: The pigment granules on biopsy could suggest pigmented basal cell carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pearly papule with rolled border and fine surface vessels**, usually on the face; palisading basaloid cells; rarely spreads
**Atypical melanocytes packed with melanin, S-100 positive, ABCDE changes in a mole**; spreads to nodes and brain

nodes.note: Both can be pigmented, so the cell of origin on biopsy decides.

nodes.q: His childhood mole could be a dysplastic nevus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Larger than 5 mm with irregular border and uneven color, but **flat and stable for years, with no invasion of the dermis by atypical cells**
**Growing and raised, with atypical melanocytes invading the dermis**

nodes.note: The trap: a dysplastic nevus shares the irregular look and is a risk marker, so only change over time and biopsy separate the two.

nodes.q: Before it changed, his mole could have passed for a compound nevus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Symmetric, smooth border, one even brown, under 6 mm, unchanged for years**; nests of bland nevus cells at the junction and in the dermis
**Asymmetric, notched border, several colors, over 6 mm and growing**; atypical cells

nodes.q: The brown color could suggest a seborrheic keratosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Waxy, 'stuck-on' brown plaque with keratin-filled horn cysts**, common with age; benign
**Smooth or nodular lesion with several colors and atypical melanin-laden cells**, no stuck-on surface

nodes.q: His years of weekly sun exposure could suggest actinic keratosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rough, sandpaper-like scaly patch on chronically sun-exposed fair skin**; dysplastic keratinocytes, no pigment-laden atypical cells
**Pigmented lesion on the sole in which melanin-laden atypical cells invade the dermis**

nodes.q: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer in Black patients. How do you tell it from his lesion?

split.note: **Scaly or ulcerated nodule that bleeds; keratin pearls and intercellular bridges** on biopsy; no melanin
**Pigmented, multicolored lesion; cells packed with melanin, S-100 positive**

nodes.q: A very dark patch could suggest a blue nevus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small, uniform steel-blue dome, stable since childhood**; benign melanocytes deep in the dermis
**Several colors, notched border and growth over time**

root.stem: A 14-year-old girl has had small rough bumps on the outer upper arms and thighs for 3 months. The bumps are skin-colored or slightly red, each centered on a hair follicle, and the skin feels like sandpaper. They do not itch or hurt, but she is embarrassed to wear sleeveless tops. She has had dry, itchy patches in her elbow creases since early childhood, and the bumps are worse each winter. There is no pus and no fever, and her armpits and groin are clear.
root.oneliner: 14F + 3 months of rough follicular bumps on outer upper arms and thighs + sandpaper feel + no itch or pain + embarrassed + childhood dry itchy elbow-crease patches + worse in winter + no pus + armpits and groin clear
highlight: bumps on the outer upper arms and thighs
dry, itchy patches in her elbow creases

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A harmless build-up of keratin in the hair follicle openings. The clincher: **painless, non-itchy, sandpaper-like follicular bumps on the outer arms and thighs in an adolescent**. It favors the extensor surfaces of the upper arms and thighs (and the cheeks in young children) and spares the palms and soles.

nodes.q: What is the underlying mechanism?
nodes.a: Plugs of keratin block the hair follicle openings (follicular hyperkeratosis)
nodes.note: Each bump is a tiny keratin plug, sometimes with a coiled hair trapped inside.

nodes.q: Which childhood skin condition, like hers, is it most often associated with?
nodes.note: Also seen with ichthyosis vulgaris. Loss-of-function changes in the filaggrin gene weaken the skin barrier in all three.

nodes.q: What is the usual course?
nodes.a: Benign and chronic; it flares in dry winter air, improves in summer and often fades with age
nodes.note: It never turns malignant and does not scar.

nodes.q: If she wants the bumps smoother, what is the first-line treatment?
nodes.a: Emollients with a keratolytic (urea, lactic acid or salicylic acid)
nodes.note: No treatment is medically required, so reassurance comes first. Keratolytics loosen the keratin plugs; topical retinoids are tried for stubborn cases.

nodes.q: Her bumps could suggest folliculitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tender or itchy red papules and pustules with a hair at the center**, from bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus) or shaving; may weep or crust
**Dry, rough, skin-colored follicular plugs with no pus, no itch and no pain**, lasting for months

nodes.note: The trap: both are bumps centered on hair follicles, but pus and pain point to infection.

nodes.q: Her bumps could suggest eczema. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Intensely itchy, red, scaly patches in the skin creases**, with scratch marks
**Non-itchy, follicle-centered bumps on the outer arms and thighs**, not in the creases

nodes.note: She has both: the elbow-crease patches are atopic dermatitis, and the bumps on the outer arms are keratosis pilaris.

nodes.q: Her bumps could suggest hidradenitis suppurativa. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painful deep nodules, abscesses and sinus tracts in the armpits, groin and under the breasts**, after puberty, with scarring
**Painless superficial bumps on the outer arms and thighs; armpits and groin clear**

nodes.q: Her bumps could suggest urticaria. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Itchy raised wheals that come and go within 24 hours**, each lasting hours
**Fixed, non-itchy follicular bumps that last for months**

root.stem: A 66-year-old man who has farmed all his life has had rough patches on his bald scalp, ears, nose and the backs of his forearms for 8 years. The patches are pink-brown, 3 to 6 mm across, and feel like sandpaper. They do not itch, but he sometimes picks at them and they bleed slightly. He has fair skin, burns easily and never wears a hat. None is ulcerated, none is larger than 1 cm, and none has grown quickly.
root.oneliner: 66M + farmer + 8 years of rough sandpaper-like pink-brown patches on bald scalp, ears, nose and forearms + no itch, bleeds when picked + fair skin, burns easily, no hat + none ulcerated, over 1 cm or fast growing
highlight: bald scalp, ears, nose and the backs of his forearms

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A precancerous patch of sun-damaged skin. The clincher: **rough, sandpaper-like scaly patches on chronically sun-exposed skin (bald scalp, ears, face, backs of hands and forearms) in an older, fair-skinned person**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same lesion. Avoid 'senile keratosis', which is also used for seborrheic keratosis.

nodes.q: Which wavelength of light causes the damage?
nodes.note: UVB forms thymine (pyrimidine) dimers in keratinocyte DNA and causes p53 mutations, producing dysplasia in the lower epidermis above scarred, sun-damaged dermis. Pigment-laden atypical cells are not seen.

nodes.q: Which cancer can it progress to?
nodes.note: Only a small fraction of lesions progress each year, but most squamous cell carcinomas of the skin begin in one. It rarely becomes basal cell carcinoma or melanoma.

nodes.q: Which change in a lesion should prompt a biopsy?
nodes.a: Thickening, ulceration, rapid growth, pain or persistent bleeding
nodes.note: These suggest invasion. His lesions have none of these.

nodes.q: What is the first-line treatment for a few lesions?
nodes.note: For many lesions across a field, topical drugs are used.

nodes.q: Which topical drug treats a whole sun-damaged field?
nodes.note: Causes redness, crusting and erosion for a few weeks while the dysplastic cells die. Imiquimod, a toll-like receptor 7 agonist that recruits local immune cells, is an alternative.

nodes.q: Which enzyme does fluorouracil inhibit?
nodes.note: The uracil analog blocks the conversion of deoxyuridine monophosphate to thymidine monophosphate, so DNA cannot be made and fast-dividing dysplastic cells die.

nodes.q: His lesions could suggest squamous cell carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Firm, rapidly growing nodule or non-healing ulcer; full-thickness atypia with invasion and keratin pearls**
**Flat, rough patches present for years, dysplasia limited to the lower epidermis, no invasion**

nodes.note: The trap: it is the cancer an actinic keratosis can become, so thickness, ulceration and growth separate them.

nodes.q: His lesions could suggest basal cell carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pearly papule with rolled border and fine surface vessels**, often a central ulcer; palisading basaloid cells
**Multiple rough, scaly, sandpaper-like patches**

nodes.q: His lesions could suggest seborrheic keratosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Waxy, 'stuck-on' brown plaque with horn cysts**; benign and not premalignant
**Dry, rough, scaly patch on sun-exposed skin; premalignant**

nodes.q: His scaly patches could suggest psoriasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sharply demarcated, thick silvery-scaled plaques on the elbows and knees, with pinpoint bleeding when the scale is removed**
**Small rough patches limited to sun-exposed skin**

nodes.q: His scaly patches could suggest tinea corporis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Itchy ring-shaped plaque with a scaly advancing edge and central clearing**; potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation shows branching hyphae
**Small, non-itchy, rough patches fixed on sun-exposed skin for years**

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching picture of a bald scalp and ear of an older fair-skinned man with several rough scaly pink-brown patches, with a small inset of dysplastic cells in the lower epidermis; no text.

root.stem: A healthy 4-month-old girl is brought in for a bright red soft lump on the right upper eyelid. It was not there at birth, appeared as a small red spot at 2 weeks of age, and has tripled in size over the past 3 weeks. It is raised and lobulated with a strawberry surface and does not bleed. It partly covers her right eye when she looks forward. She has no other skin lesions and no noisy breathing.
root.oneliner: 4-month-old F + red spot at 2 weeks, absent at birth + tripled in 3 weeks + raised lobulated strawberry surface, no bleeding + partly covers right eye + no other lesions, no noisy breathing
highlight: small red spot at 2 weeks of age
tripled in size over the past 3 weeks
raised and lobulated with a strawberry surface

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common tumor of infancy. The clincher: **a red lump absent at birth that appears in the first weeks, grows quickly for months, then shrinks on its own**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All names describe the same tumor.

nodes.q: Which marker on its endothelial cells separates it from vascular malformations?
nodes.note: The tumor is a proliferation of capillary endothelial cells that are GLUT1 positive at every stage; vascular malformations (such as a port-wine stain) are GLUT1 negative.

nodes.q: What is expected over the next 5 years?
nodes.note: Rapid growth lasts about the first 5 to 6 months (most growth is done by 5 months), then the lesion slowly fades; involution is complete in most children by about age 4. It does not spread, turn malignant or involve internal organs, and may leave loose fibrofatty skin or fine vessels.

nodes.q: Which vision problem threatens a child with a lesion like this one?
nodes.note: A lesion over the eye can block the visual axis or distort the cornea. Ophthalmology review is urgent.

nodes.q: Which drug shrinks a hemangioma that threatens vision?
nodes.note: It constricts vessels, lowers growth-factor signalling and triggers endothelial apoptosis. Topical timolol suits small superficial lesions.

nodes.q: She has a single lesion. Which organ is imaged when an infant has five or more skin hemangiomas?
nodes.a: The liver (abdominal ultrasound for hepatic hemangiomas)
nodes.note: Many hepatic hemangiomas can cause heart failure from shunting and hypothyroidism from tumor-made type 3 deiodinase.

nodes.q: Her red lesion could suggest a port-wine stain. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Flat pink-red patch present at birth that never regresses**, grows with the child, GLUT1 negative; on the forehead or upper eyelid it can signal Sturge-Weber syndrome
**Absent at birth; raised strawberry lump that grows for months, then involutes**

nodes.note: The trap: both are red vascular birthmarks near the eye, but only one is present at birth and stays.

nodes.q: Her lesion could suggest a pyogenic granuloma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Friable red papule that bleeds easily after minor injury**, usually in older children, adults and pregnancy, on the face, lips or fingers, with a collarette of scale; it rarely regresses
**Appears in the first weeks of life, does not bleed, then regresses by itself**

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching picture of a 4-month-old girl with a raised bright red lobulated strawberry-like lump on the right upper eyelid partly covering the eye, with a small inset of a growth curve rising then falling over years; no text.

root.stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with a 4-day painful rash. Nine days ago she began trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a bladder infection. Two days before the rash she had fever, sore throat and body aches. The rash began on her chest as dusky red flat spots, then spread to her face, arms and legs and now covers about 40% of her body surface with blisters. Her mouth, eyes and lips have painful erosions. The top layer of skin on uninvolved-looking areas peels away with gentle sideways pressure. Temperature is 39.0°C and pulse is 120/min. A skin biopsy shows death of keratinocytes through the full thickness of the epidermis with very few lymphocytes in the upper dermis.
root.oneliner: 34F + trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 9 days ago + fever, sore throat and body aches prodrome + painful dusky rash spreading to cover 40% of body surface with blisters + mouth, eye and lip erosions + skin peels with sideways pressure + full-thickness epidermal necrosis with few lymphocytes
highlight: fever, sore throat and body aches
peels away with gentle sideways pressure

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most severe form of the Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) spectrum. The clincher: **a drug started 1 to 3 weeks earlier + painful mucosal erosions + skin sloughing over more than 30% of the body + full-thickness epidermal necrosis with little inflammation**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: What extent of skin detachment separates it from Stevens-Johnson syndrome?
nodes.a: More than 30% of body surface (Stevens-Johnson syndrome is under 10%; 10 to 30% is overlap)
nodes.note: She has about 40%.

nodes.q: Which bedside sign does her sliding skin show?
nodes.a: Nikolsky sign (skin shears off with sideways pressure)
nodes.note: Also positive in pemphigus vulgaris and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, so it does not decide the diagnosis alone.

nodes.q: What is the mechanism?
nodes.a: Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity: cytotoxic T cells release granulysin and Fas ligand, causing keratinocyte apoptosis and separation at the dermal-epidermal junction
nodes.note: This explains full-thickness necrosis with sparse inflammation.

nodes.q: Which drug class is her likely trigger?
nodes.note: Other classic triggers: allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine), nevirapine and some nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Onset is typically 4 days to 4 weeks after starting the drug. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the main non-drug trigger, mostly in children.

nodes.q: Which allele predicts carbamazepine-induced disease in people of Han Chinese descent?
nodes.note: Screen before starting carbamazepine in at-risk groups. HLA-B*58:01 predicts allopurinol-induced disease.

nodes.q: What is the main cause of death?
nodes.a: Sepsis from the denuded skin, with fluid and electrolyte loss
nodes.note: Treat like an extensive burn.

nodes.q: What is the first step in management?
nodes.a: Stop the culprit drug at once and transfer to a burn unit
nodes.note: Supportive care: fluids, wound care, pain control, nutrition and early ophthalmology review. Systemic steroids are not clearly beneficial.

nodes.q: Which immunosuppressant is most often added to halt the T-cell attack?
nodes.note: Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin and inhibits calcineurin, blocking interleukin-2 production and T-cell activation. Intravenous immunoglobulin and etanercept are alternatives.

nodes.q: Which late complication threatens vision?
nodes.a: Ocular scarring: symblepharon, corneal scarring and dry eye
nodes.note: Survivors often need long-term eye care.

nodes.q: Her peeling skin could suggest staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Child under 5 with fever and tender red skin; **mouth and eyes spared; split high in the granular layer** by staphylococcal exfoliative toxin; no drug trigger
Adult after a drug; **mucosal erosions + full-thickness epidermal necrosis** at the dermal-epidermal junction

nodes.note: The trap: both have a positive Nikolsky sign, so histology and the mucosal erosions decide.

nodes.q: Her rash could suggest erythema multiforme. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Target lesions with three zones** after herpes simplex virus or Mycoplasma; under 10% involvement, mild mouth lesions, no sloughing
**Dusky flat macules, mucosal erosions and sloughing over more than 30%** after a drug

nodes.q: Her mouth erosions could suggest pemphigus vulgaris. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Flaccid blisters that rupture into erosions, mouth first**, over weeks; acantholysis and IgG against desmoglein 3 in a net-like pattern; no drug trigger
**Days after a drug, with full-thickness necrosis and no acantholysis**

nodes.q: Her blisters could suggest linear IgA bullous dermatosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tense subepidermal blisters in a 'string of pearls' ring**, often after vancomycin; linear IgA along the basement membrane
**Dusky macules with sheet-like sloughing, mucosal erosions and full-thickness necrosis** after trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching picture of a woman's back with dusky red flat patches, blisters and sheets of peeling skin, with a small inset showing the whole epidermis necrotic over an intact dermis; no text.

root.stem: A 6-year-old boy has had many small bumps on his trunk and armpits for 3 months. The bumps are skin-colored, shiny and dome-shaped, 2 to 4 mm across, each with a tiny central dimple. Some are slightly itchy and a few have a red rim. When one is squeezed, a white cheesy core comes out. He swims at a community pool twice a week, and his younger brother has two similar bumps. He is otherwise healthy, has no burrows between his fingers, no scaly ring-shaped patches and no pale, finely scaly patches on his back.
root.oneliner: 6M + 3 months of many skin-colored, shiny, dome-shaped 2-4 mm bumps with a central dimple on trunk and armpits + white cheesy core when squeezed + community pool + brother with similar bumps + no burrows, no scaly rings, no pale scaly patches
highlight: younger brother has two similar bumps
no pale, finely scaly patches on his back

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A common, harmless skin infection of children. The clincher: **shiny, dome-shaped, skin-colored papules with a central dimple (umbilication) that release a white cheesy core**.

nodes.q: What is seen on microscopic examination of the expressed core?
nodes.a: Molluscum bodies (Henderson-Patterson bodies): large eosinophilic inclusions inside keratinocytes
nodes.note: These are viral inclusions packed with virions.

nodes.q: Which virus causes it?
nodes.a: Molluscum contagiosum virus, a poxvirus (a large DNA virus that replicates in the cytoplasm)
nodes.note: Poxviruses are unusual because they replicate outside the nucleus.

nodes.q: How does it spread?
nodes.a: By skin contact, shared towels and pool equipment, and by scratching it onto new sites (autoinoculation)
nodes.note: In adults it is also spread by sexual contact.

nodes.q: In which immunodeficiency do lesions become large, numerous and persistent?
nodes.a: Advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection with a low CD4 count
nodes.note: Giant lesions on the adult face should prompt HIV testing.

nodes.q: What does a red, inflamed rim around a lesion signal?
nodes.a: The immune system is attacking the virus and the lesion is about to clear
nodes.note: Sometimes called the beginning of the end. Itchy, red skin around lesions can also be molluscum dermatitis.

nodes.q: What is the natural course?
nodes.a: Self-limited: it clears without scarring, usually in 6 to 12 months, occasionally up to 4 years
nodes.note: Observation is a reasonable choice.

nodes.q: What treatment is used when the family wants one?
nodes.note: Cantharidin is a blistering agent applied in the office. Aggressive treatment can scar.

nodes.q: His itchy bumps could suggest scabies. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Intense night-time itch with burrows in the finger webs and wrists**; scraping shows mites, eggs and feces
**Painless to mildly itchy dome-shaped papules with a central dimple**; no burrows

nodes.q: His red-rimmed lesions could suggest tinea. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Scaly ring-shaped plaque with central clearing**; potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation shows branching hyphae
**Smooth shiny dome-shaped papules, not scaly rings**; core shows molluscum bodies

nodes.q: Bumps in his armpits could suggest candidiasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Beefy-red, moist patches in skin folds with satellite pustules**; KOH shows budding yeast and pseudohyphae
**Firm skin-colored papules with a central dimple, not a moist red patch**

nodes.q: Spots on his trunk could suggest tinea versicolor. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Flat pale or tan, finely scaly patches on the upper trunk**; KOH shows short hyphae and small round yeast ('spaghetti and meatballs') of Malassezia
**Raised, dome-shaped papules with a central dimple**; the core shows molluscum bodies, not fungus

nodes.q: His bumps could suggest common warts. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rough, keratotic surface with black dots of thrombosed capillaries**; no central dimple or cheesy core
**Smooth, shiny, dimpled papules with a white cheesy core**

nodes.note: The trap: both are contagious viral bumps in children, but the surface and the core differ.

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching picture of a close-up of a child's inner upper arm near the armpit, T-shirt sleeve pushed up, with several shiny skin-colored dome-shaped bumps with central dimples, one releasing a white core, with a small inset of a large inclusion body in a keratinocyte; no text.

root.stem: A 29-year-old woman who works as a laboratory technician has had an itchy red rash on both hands for 4 days. Two weeks ago her lab switched to a new brand of rubber (latex) gloves, which she wears for most of her shift, and last month she changed to a cheaper laundry detergent. Small clear blisters are scattered over the backs of both hands and the rash ends sharply at the wrist creases, with normal skin above and on the rest of her body. The blisters are itchy, not painful. She has no hives, wheezing or lip swelling. Coworkers who wear the same gloves have no rash. She has no history of asthma, hay fever or childhood eczema. Last summer, after clearing brush at her cabin, she had streaks of itchy blisters on both shins.
root.oneliner: 29F + lab technician + itchy rash on both hands for 4 days + new brand of latex gloves 2 weeks ago + new laundry detergent last month + scattered clear blisters ending sharply at the wrist creases + no hives, wheezing or lip swelling + coworkers with the same gloves unaffected + no asthma, hay fever or childhood eczema + streaks of blisters on the shins after clearing brush
highlight: itchy red rash on both hands
changed to a cheaper laundry detergent
ends sharply at the wrist creases
normal skin above and on the rest of her body
no hives, wheezing or lip swelling
Coworkers who wear the same gloves have no rash
no history of asthma, hay fever or childhood eczema
streaks of itchy blisters on both shins

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A delayed skin reaction to a substance the immune system was sensitized to earlier. The clincher: **itchy blistering rash confined to the skin that touched the allergen, starting 1-2 days after re-exposure**. Stems often shorten the name to 'contact dermatitis'.

nodes.q: Which of her exposures is the likely trigger?
nodes.note: The rash stops sharply at the wrist creases, exactly where the glove cuff ends; a detergent rash would involve clothed skin of the trunk and thighs. In glove dermatitis the type IV allergen is usually a chemical added during rubber manufacture (accelerators such as thiurams); the exam usually just says 'latex gloves'. Other common triggers: nickel, neomycin, fragrances, hair dye (p-phenylenediamine) and plant oils. Occupational exposure is the classic setting.

nodes.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
nodes.note: T-cell mediated, with no antibody or complement involved. The first exposure sensitizes; the rash appears 24-72 hours after the next contact.

nodes.q: Which skin cell picks up the hapten-bound protein and carries it to the lymph node?
nodes.a: Langerhans cell (a dendritic cell of the epidermis)
nodes.note: The small chemical (hapten) binds skin proteins; the Langerhans cell presents it on major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II to CD4+ T helper cells.

nodes.q: Which receptor-ligand pair gives the second signal that lets the T cell proliferate?
nodes.a: CD28 on the T cell binding CD80 (B7-1) on the Langerhans cell
nodes.note: Signal 1 is the T-cell receptor seeing hapten-peptide on MHC class II; signal 2 is CD28 binding B7 (CD80/CD86). Without it the T cell becomes anergic; with it the T cell makes interleukin-2 and proliferates into memory cells. Look-alike pairs: CD2 binding LFA-3 or ICAM-3 and LFA-1 binding ICAM-1 are adhesion, not the proliferation signal; CD40 ligand binding CD40 licenses the antigen-presenting cell and drives B-cell class switching; CD45 is a phosphatase, not a ligand for CD28.

nodes.q: On re-exposure, which cells and messengers produce the blisters?
nodes.a: Memory T lymphocytes releasing cytokines that activate macrophages
nodes.note: CD4+ T helper 1 cells release interferon-gamma, which recruits and activates macrophages and stimulates keratinocytes; CD8+ T cells add direct keratinocyte killing. The skin shows lymphocytes and fluid between epidermal cells (spongiosis). No antibody, complement, immune complexes, IgE or mast cells are involved.

nodes.q: Her shin streaks came from a plant. Which plant oil causes this same reaction?
nodes.note: Linear streaks of blisters come from the brushing of leaves across skin. Fluid from the blisters does not spread the rash.

nodes.q: Which test finds the culprit allergen?
nodes.a: Patch testing, read at 48 and 96 hours
nodes.note: Standard allergen patches are taped to the back; a raised, red, blistered spot marks a positive.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Avoid the allergen and apply a topical corticosteroid
nodes.note: A short oral prednisone taper is used for severe or widespread disease. Nitrile gloves replace latex.

nodes.q: Where in the arachidonic acid pathway do corticosteroids act to cut inflammation?
nodes.a: They induce annexin A1 (lipocortin), which inhibits phospholipase A2, so less arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipids
nodes.note: Fewer prostaglandins and leukotrienes follow. Corticosteroids also reduce cyclooxygenase-2 expression; NSAIDs block only cyclooxygenase.

nodes.q: Her gloves could suggest latex allergy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Immunoglobulin E (IgE) on mast cells. **Hives, lip swelling or wheezing within minutes of contact**
T cells. **Itchy blisters limited to the contact area, appearing 1-2 days later; no hives or wheeze**

nodes.note: The trap: both come from latex gloves, but one is immediate and antibody-driven, the other delayed and cell-driven.

nodes.q: Hand rash after glove use could suggest irritant contact dermatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Direct chemical damage, no sensitization needed. **Dry, cracked, burning skin in many exposed coworkers**
Needs prior sensitization. **Itchy blisters in one person while coworkers with the same exposure are spared**; patch test positive

nodes.q: A hand rash with itch could suggest atopic dermatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Starts in childhood; flexures; **personal or family history of asthma, hay fever or eczema**; chronic and relapsing
Adult onset; **follows the shape of the exposure with no atopic history**; clears when the allergen is removed

nodes.q: Blisters on the hands could suggest herpes simplex infection. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Grouped, painful vesicles on a red base**, usually one site; Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells
**Scattered itchy blisters on both hands in a glove pattern**, not painful or grouped

root.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had an itchy rash for 1 week. It began as a single 4 cm oval, salmon-colored scaly patch on her abdomen. Five days later many smaller oval pink scaly patches appeared on her back, chest and upper arms, with their long axes running along the skin lines. She has had no fever, sore throat or mouth sores. Her palms and soles are clear. She has had one sexual partner for 2 years and uses an oral contraceptive. She has no burrows, no swollen glands and no recent illness in family members.
root.oneliner: 24F + 1 week of itchy rash + one 4 cm oval salmon scaly patch on the abdomen first + many smaller oval patches on the trunk along skin lines 5 days later + no fever + palms and soles clear + one long-term partner + no burrows or family illness
highlight: single 4 cm oval, salmon-colored scaly patch on her abdomen
smaller oval pink scaly patches appeared on her back, chest and upper arms
long axes running along the skin lines
no fever, sore throat or mouth sores

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A self-limited rash of young adults. The clincher: **a single herald patch followed days later by smaller oval scaly patches along skin lines on the trunk**.

nodes.q: What is the name of the first lesion that heralds the eruption?
nodes.note: A larger oval salmon plaque with a fine ring of scale just inside its edge (collarette scale), usually on the trunk. It often precedes the other patches by 1-2 weeks.

nodes.q: What is the name of the pattern these patches make on her back?
nodes.note: Each oval patch lies with its long axis along the skin cleavage (Langer) lines, which slope down and out from the spine like the branches of a fir tree.

nodes.q: Which viruses are thought to reactivate to cause it?
nodes.note: It is not contagious. Rash often follows a mild upper respiratory illness.

nodes.q: How long does it last without treatment?
nodes.a: 6 to 8 weeks, then it clears on its own
nodes.note: Reassurance is the main treatment. Topical corticosteroids or oral antihistamines help the itch. Evidence for erythromycin or acyclovir is limited.

nodes.q: Which blood test is worth ordering in a sexually active patient with a trunk rash like this?
nodes.note: The rash can mimic secondary syphilis, and syphilis is the diagnosis you cannot afford to miss.

nodes.q: Her trunk rash could suggest secondary syphilis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rash on the palms and soles + swollen glands + mouth patches or a past painless sore**; positive serology
**Herald patch first, then oval patches along skin lines; palms and soles clear**; serology negative

nodes.note: The trap: both are scaly pink trunk rashes in a sexually active young adult.

nodes.q: A pink rash could suggest erythema infectiosum (fifth disease). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Parvovirus B19, school-age child. **Bright red 'slapped cheeks' then a lacy rash on the limbs**
Young adult. **Herald patch and scaly oval patches on the trunk; no slapped cheeks**

nodes.q: A rash on the trunk could suggest roseola. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Infant with **high fever for 3 days, then rash appears as the fever breaks**
Young adult with **no fever; itchy scaly oval patches**

nodes.q: Her small skin lesions could suggest molluscum contagiosum. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Flesh-colored dome papules with a central dimple (umbilication)**; poxvirus; not scaly ovals
**Oval pink patches with a ring of scale along skin lines**, no central dimple

nodes.q: An itchy rash could suggest scabies. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Itch worst at night, burrows in finger webs and wrists, household contacts itching**
**Herald patch then trunk-only oval patches; no burrows and no itchy contacts**

root.stem: A 7-year-old girl has had an intensely itchy rash for 2 weeks that is worst at night and keeps her awake. Examination shows small red papules, several with thin gray wavy lines, and many scratch marks in the finger webs, both wrists, the armpits and the waistline. Her 4-year-old brother and her mother have started to itch. The family camped in the woods last month and she found no tick. She has no history of eczema and the family has not changed soaps. A scraping of one lesion in mineral oil is taken.
root.oneliner: 7F + 2 weeks of intense itch worse at night + red papules with thin gray wavy lines in finger webs, wrists, armpits, waistline + scratch marks + brother and mother itching + camping last month with no tick + no eczema or new soaps
highlight: intensely itchy rash for 2 weeks that is worst at night
finger webs, both wrists, the armpits and the waistline
Her 4-year-old brother and her mother have started to itch
camped in the woods last month and she found no tick

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An infestation of the skin by a mite. The clincher: **intense night-time itch + burrows in the finger webs and wrists + itching in household contacts**.

nodes.q: How is it spread from person to person?
nodes.a: Prolonged skin-to-skin contact, usually within a household
nodes.note: So the most useful question to a parent is whether anyone else in the family has an itchy rash. Pets, travel, medicines and new soaps do not explain it. Exterminators, insect repellent and long clothing outdoors do not help.

nodes.q: Where in the skin does the female mite live and lay her eggs?
nodes.a: In a burrow in the stratum corneum (the outermost layer of the epidermis)
nodes.note: The mite is Sarcoptes scabiei. Her burrow is the thin gray wavy line. The itch is a delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, its eggs and its feces, so it starts 2-6 weeks after a first infestation (1-3 days after a repeat one).

nodes.q: What does a skin scraping show?
nodes.a: Mites, eggs or fecal pellets (scybala) under the microscope
nodes.note: Mineral oil placed on a burrow before scraping keeps the material together.

nodes.q: Which drug is first-line treatment?
nodes.note: Applied from the neck down, washed off after 8-14 hours and repeated in 1 week. Bedding and clothes are washed in hot water.

nodes.q: How does permethrin kill the mite?
nodes.a: It blocks inactivation of the mite's nerve sodium channels, so the nerves keep firing and the mite is paralyzed
nodes.note: Little is absorbed through human skin and it is quickly broken down, so it is safe in children over 2 months.

nodes.q: Who else needs treatment at the same time?
nodes.a: All household members and close contacts, even those without symptoms
nodes.note: Otherwise the mites are passed back and forth.

nodes.q: Which oral drug is the alternative?
nodes.note: It is used for crusted scabies, institutional outbreaks, or when permethrin fails.

nodes.q: How does ivermectin kill the mite?
nodes.a: It opens glutamate-gated chloride channels, paralyzing the mite
nodes.note: Mammals have no glutamate-gated chloride channels, and the blood-brain barrier keeps the drug away from the human GABA-gated channels it can also open.

nodes.q: Which bacterial skin infection can complicate the scratching?
nodes.note: Itching breaks the skin and lets bacteria in.

nodes.q: Which kidney disease can follow a streptococcal skin infection?
nodes.note: Cola-colored urine, edema and high blood pressure 3-6 weeks after a streptococcal skin infection (1-3 weeks after a throat infection). Treating impetigo does not prevent it.

nodes.q: In which patients does it form a thick crust holding millions of mites?
nodes.a: Immunocompromised, elderly or institutionalized patients (crusted, or Norwegian, scabies)
nodes.note: It is highly contagious and needs ivermectin plus a topical agent.

nodes.q: What happens to the itch after the mites are killed?
nodes.a: It can persist for 2 to 4 weeks
nodes.note: The immune reaction to dead mite material fades slowly; antihistamines or topical steroids help.

nodes.q: Camping in the woods could suggest Lyme disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Tick bite, then **expanding red ring with central clearing (erythema migrans)**, usually not itchy
**Intense night-time itch with finger-web burrows and itching household members**; no tick bite

nodes.note: The trap: the woods exposure points the wrong way; the family itch points to person-to-person spread.

nodes.q: Her scratch marks could suggest atopic dermatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Flexures and face; **personal or family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever**; no burrows; contacts unaffected
**Burrows in finger webs and waistline with itching contacts**; no eczema history

nodes.q: A new itchy rash could suggest contact dermatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Follows the shape of the exposure after a **new soap, plant or glove**; contacts unaffected
**Wavy burrows with itch spreading to family members; no new soaps**

nodes.q: Itchy red papules could suggest insect bites. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Clusters or lines on exposed skin**, no burrows, and household members are not infected with a transmissible rash
**Papules with burrows in the finger webs, wrists and waistline, spreading through the household**

The rest of his skin is normal, his delivery was uncomplicated with no bruising, and his parents have no history of skin or nerve tumors.

present since the first day of life
not raised, not hairy and not red
has not changed color over the week
no history of skin or nerve tumors

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A flat, evenly pigmented patch the color of milky coffee. The clincher: **flat, uniform tan-brown macule with smooth edges, present from birth or early infancy**.

nodes.q: What causes the color?
nodes.a: More melanin in the basal keratinocytes of the epidermis, with a normal number of melanocytes
nodes.note: In neurofibromatosis the melanosomes are enlarged (macromelanosomes).

nodes.q: How many spots, and of what size, raise suspicion for neurofibromatosis type 1?
nodes.a: Six or more spots larger than 5 mm before puberty (larger than 15 mm after puberty)
nodes.note: One or two spots occur in about 10-20% of healthy people.

nodes.q: Which other findings complete the diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) as the child grows?
nodes.a: Axillary or groin freckling, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas), optic glioma
nodes.note: Autosomal dominant, from a mutation in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17. Its protein, neurofibromin, is a tumor suppressor that switches Ras off (a GTPase-activating protein), so loss keeps Ras active.

nodes.q: What is the plan for a single spot in a well infant?
nodes.a: Reassure and follow the child's skin over time
nodes.note: Examine for axillary freckling and new spots at each visit and ask about family history; refer for slit-lamp and genetic evaluation if the count rises.

nodes.q: A pigmented patch present at birth could suggest a congenital melanocytic nevus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Brown to black, often **raised, textured or hairy** and darker in places; a large one carries melanoma risk
**Flat, evenly tan, smooth-edged, hairless**

nodes.note: The trap: both are present at birth and brown.

nodes.q: A birth patch with color could suggest a slate gray nevus (dermal melanocytosis). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Blue-gray patch**, usually over the lower back or buttocks; melanocytes deep in the dermis
**Tan-brown with no blue-gray tint**; pigment in the epidermis

nodes.q: A birth mark on the flank could suggest a hemangioma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Red, raised, strawberry-like**; grows in the first months then involutes
**Flat and tan-brown, not red, and stays the same**

nodes.q: A skin patch in a newborn could suggest ecchymosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: After a difficult delivery; **changes color from purple to green to yellow and fades within days**
**Uniform tan-brown that does not change or fade**; no birth trauma

nodes.q: A brown mark could suggest an acquired melanocytic nevus or melanoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Appears after infancy; round, small mole; melanoma is asymmetric with irregular border and color change**
**Present in the first days of life, flat, smooth and uniform**

nodes.q: A large tan birth patch could suggest McCune-Albright syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Large spot with a jagged ('coast of Maine') border, often on one side of the body**, with precocious puberty and fibrous dysplasia of bone; mosaic GNAS mutation
**Single small spot with a smooth ('coast of California') border** in a well infant; the smooth border is also the NF1 type

root.stem: A 36-year-old man has had an extremely itchy rash for 6 weeks on his elbows, knees, buttocks and scalp. Most lesions are crusted red bumps with scratch marks, and a few small clear blisters are grouped on the buttocks. He has had bloating and loose stools for 3 years, worse after bread and pasta, and he is mildly anemic. A biopsy of a blister shows the split lies beneath the epidermis (subepidermal); a biopsy of normal-looking skin beside a lesion, studied with direct immunofluorescence, shows granular immunoglobulin A (IgA) deposits at the tips of the dermal papillae.

highlight: crusted red bumps with scratch marks
bloating and loose stools for 3 years
granular immunoglobulin A (IgA) deposits at the tips of the dermal papillae

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An itchy blistering skin disease that is the skin form of gluten sensitivity. The clincher: **intensely itchy grouped bumps and blisters on extensor surfaces and buttocks + granular IgA at the dermal papillae**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: On routine histology of an early lesion, which cell collects at the tips of the dermal papillae?
nodes.note: They sit just below a subepidermal split. The diagnostic test is direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin showing granular IgA at the papillary tips, as in his biopsy.

nodes.q: Which gut disease is nearly always present?
nodes.note: Linked to human leukocyte antigen (HLA) DQ2 and DQ8. Gluten drives the IgA response.

nodes.q: Which antigen does the skin IgA target?
nodes.note: It cross-reacts with the tissue transglutaminase targeted in celiac disease.

nodes.q: Which skin should be biopsied for direct immunofluorescence?
nodes.a: Normal-looking skin next to a lesion (perilesional skin)
nodes.note: Blister fluid and scratched lesions destroy the IgA deposits.

nodes.q: Which blood tests support the diagnosis?
nodes.a: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies
nodes.note: A small-bowel biopsy is not needed if the skin biopsy is typical.

nodes.q: Which diet controls the skin and gut disease?
nodes.note: Skin clears slowly over months to years, so a drug is added at first.

nodes.q: Which drug clears the itch within days?
nodes.note: Dapsone reduces neutrophil recruitment and their myeloperoxidase damage; as an antibacterial it blocks folate synthesis (dihydropteroate synthase). Check glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) first, because it causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. It also causes methemoglobinemia.

nodes.q: Which cancer is the long-term risk of untreated gluten sensitivity?
nodes.a: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma of the small bowel
nodes.note: Other associations: autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes.

nodes.q: Subepidermal blisters could suggest bullous pemphigoid. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Older adults, **large tense bullae + linear immunoglobulin G (IgG) and complement C3 along the basement membrane**; antibodies to BP180
Young to middle-aged adult, **tiny itchy blisters on elbows, knees and buttocks + granular IgA at papillary tips**

nodes.note: The trap: both are subepidermal blistering diseases.

nodes.q: A blistering disease on the extensor surfaces could suggest epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Blisters at sites of trauma, scarring; linear IgG against type VII collagen**
**Itchy papulovesicles with granular IgA, improved by gluten-free diet**

nodes.q: A blistering skin disease could suggest pemphigus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Flaccid intraepidermal blisters, painful mouth erosions; net-like IgG between keratinocytes**
**Subepidermal, intensely itchy, no mouth erosions; granular IgA**

nodes.q: Small itchy blisters could suggest dyshidrotic eczema. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Deep tapioca-like vesicles on the palms, soles and sides of fingers**; no IgA
**Elbows, knees, buttocks and scalp; gluten-related bowel symptoms**

root.stem: A 26-year-old man has had a painful, swollen lump on the back of his left forearm for 2 days, where a sliver of wood lodged while he was building a fence. He is otherwise healthy and takes no medicines.
root.oneliner: 26M + 2 days of painful swollen lump on the forearm at a wood splinter + red, warm, tender + 3 cm fluctuant center with yellow point + no streaking + temperature 37.8°C
highlight: painful, swollen lump on the back of his left forearm for 2 days
3 cm soft fluctuant center with a central yellow spot

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A walled-off pocket of pus in the skin. The clincher: **tender, warm, fluctuant swelling with a central pus point after skin penetration**.

nodes.q: Which organism is the most common cause?
nodes.a: Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)
nodes.note: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase and coagulase positive. Its coagulase helps wall off the pus.

nodes.q: Which cell fills the pus?
nodes.note: Dead neutrophils, bacteria and liquefied tissue; the wall is fibrous and granulation tissue.

nodes.q: Which endothelial molecules first catch passing leukocytes at the site and make them roll?
nodes.note: They bind sialyl Lewis X on the leukocyte. P-selectin is released from Weibel-Palade bodies within minutes of histamine or thrombin; E-selectin is made over hours in response to tumor necrosis factor-alpha and interleukin-1.

nodes.q: Which molecules then hold the leukocyte firmly?
nodes.a: Integrins on the leukocyte (such as LFA-1) binding intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1) on the endothelium
nodes.note: Then the cell squeezes between endothelial cells (diapedesis, using platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule 1, PECAM-1) and follows chemotaxis, for example to interleukin-8 and C5a. Defective integrin (CD18) causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency: delayed umbilical cord separation and infections without pus.

nodes.q: What is the primary treatment?
nodes.note: Antibiotics alone do not penetrate the pus-filled cavity.

nodes.q: When are antibiotics added after drainage?
nodes.a: Spreading cellulitis, fever or systemic signs, immunosuppression or a very young or old patient
nodes.note: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or doxycycline covers MRSA; vancomycin if severe.

nodes.q: What can an untreated abscess lead to?
nodes.a: **Bacteremia and sepsis** or spread into deeper tissue
nodes.note: Also cellulitis, lymphangitis and, on the hand, a deep space infection.

nodes.q: The red swelling could suggest cellulitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Spreading, poorly demarcated redness without a fluctuant pus collection**; Streptococcus pyogenes; antibiotics alone
**Fluctuant, well-defined collection with a central pus point**; needs drainage

nodes.note: The trap: an abscess is often surrounded by cellulitis.

nodes.q: A yellow pus point could suggest folliculitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small superficial pustule centered on a hair follicle**; no deep swelling

spends most of the day in bed
red, does not blanch when pressed

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Skin and tissue death over a bony prominence. The clincher: **immobile patient + non-blanching redness or sore over the sacrum, heel or hip**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All three names are used for the same lesion.

nodes.q: Which factor must be relieved first to prevent these ulcers forming?
nodes.a: Pressure: sustained pressure above capillary pressure over a bony prominence, causing ischemia
nodes.note: Shear, friction, moisture and poor nutrition add to it. Arterial flow, venous disease and skin bacteria are not the cause in this man with strong pulses.

nodes.q: Over which bony prominences do they form most often?
nodes.a: The sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities and greater trochanters
nodes.note: They are the bony prominences that bear weight when lying or sitting.

nodes.q: Which stage is the trochanteric sore, with full-thickness skin loss and visible fat but no muscle or bone?
nodes.note: Stage 1 is non-blanching redness (his sacrum). Stage 2 is partial thickness. Stage 4 exposes muscle, tendon or bone.

nodes.q: What is the routine bedside measure to prevent new ulcers?
nodes.a: Turning him at least every 2 hours on a pressure-redistributing mattress
nodes.note: Nutrition, moisture control and skin care help, but relief of pressure is first.

nodes.q: How are established ulcers treated?
nodes.a: Offload pressure, debride dead tissue, keep the wound moist and give protein
nodes.note: Surgical flap closure is used for deep stage 4 ulcers.

nodes.q: Which deep infection of the underlying bone can follow a stage 4 ulcer?
nodes.note: Diagnose with bone biopsy and culture. It can progress to sepsis. Chronic ulcers may rarely become squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer).

nodes.q: A leg or foot sore could suggest a venous stasis ulcer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Medial ankle, leg swelling, varicose veins and brown discoloration**
**Over bony prominences in an immobile patient; no swelling or varicose veins**

nodes.note: The trap: both are chronic ulcers in hospitalized patients.

nodes.q: A chronic sore could suggest an arterial ulcer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painful punched-out sore on toes or lateral foot, cool pale limb, absent pulses**
**Over weight-bearing prominences with strong pedal pulses**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma (FAMMM) syndrome
nodes.note: An inherited syndrome of many atypical moles with a very high melanoma risk. The clincher: **dozens of large irregular moles, including on sun-protected skin + melanoma in close relatives**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All names describe the same inherited condition.

nodes.q: Which skin lesion is expected on both sun-exposed and covered skin in this syndrome?
nodes.note: Larger than a common mole, with irregular borders and variable color. They are precursors and markers of melanoma risk.

nodes.q: Which gene is most often mutated?
nodes.note: Inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Loss of p16 releases the brake on cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6, so the retinoblastoma protein stays phosphorylated and cells enter S phase. CDK4 mutations are rarer.

nodes.q: When melanoma develops, which measurement best predicts spread and survival?
nodes.note: Melanoma grows first sideways (radial growth phase), then down into the dermis (vertical growth phase), when it can metastasize. Markers: S-100 and HMB-45; BRAF V600E is common. Her risk is high even on unexposed skin.

nodes.q: Which other cancer shows up in some carriers and in her father?
nodes.note: CDKN2A carriers with a family history may be offered pancreatic surveillance by MRI or endoscopic ultrasound.

nodes.q: How is the patient followed?
nodes.a: Full-body skin examination every 3 to 6 months with photographs or dermoscopy, and strict sun protection
nodes.note: Start in adolescence and screen family members.

nodes.q: How is a suspicious lesion sampled?
nodes.a: Excisional biopsy with a narrow margin
nodes.note: Shave and punch biopsies can cut through the base and ruin the Breslow depth.

nodes.note: The trap: both are brown lesions that can look irregular; seborrheic keratosis is usually in older adults and is never a melanoma precursor.

**Discrete irregular moles, not velvety folds**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A disease of the hair follicle and its oil gland (the pilosebaceous unit). The clincher: **blackheads and whiteheads with red papules and pustules on the face of an adolescent**.

nodes.q: What is the basic abnormality in the follicle?
nodes.a: Follicular plugging by overgrowth of epidermal cells, together with excess sebum production
nodes.note: The follicle lining overproduces cells that block the opening, and oil builds up behind the plug. Diet, chocolate and makeup are not the cause.

nodes.q: What is the name of the non-inflamed plugged follicle seen as her blackheads and whiteheads?
nodes.note: An open comedo is dark because of oxidized melanin and keratin, not dirt.

nodes.q: Which hormones switch on the oil glands at puberty?
nodes.note: They enlarge the sebaceous glands and increase sebum. In girls the first source is the adrenal gland; boys add testosterone from the testes.

nodes.q: Which adrenal layer makes dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), the androgen that rises at adrenarche?
nodes.note: Adrenarche (about age 6-8) comes before the rise of gonadal hormones; DHEA and its sulfate are the adrenal androgens.

nodes.q: Which skin bacterium living in the plugged follicle drives the inflammation?
nodes.note: Formerly called Propionibacterium acnes. It breaks down sebum into free fatty acids that attract neutrophils.

nodes.q: Which part of her daily life best explains why the lesions sit on the forehead?
nodes.a: Friction and occlusion from the helmet
nodes.note: Called acne mechanica. Her diet, chocolate, the new pet and sun exposure do not cause acne.

nodes.q: Which permanent skin change can deep inflamed lesions leave behind?
nodes.note: Early treatment matters because scars are permanent.

nodes.q: Which topical drug class is used first to unplug the follicles?
nodes.note: Often combined with benzoyl peroxide. Retinoids normalize follicular cell turnover.

nodes.q: Which oral antibiotic class was she most likely taking, given that milk stopped it working?
nodes.note: Used for moderate inflammatory acne: they lower C. acnes numbers and have an anti-inflammatory effect. Avoid in pregnancy and under age 8 (tooth discoloration).

nodes.q: Why did the drug stop working once she took it with milk?
nodes.a: Calcium in milk binds (chelates) the drug and blocks its absorption
nodes.note: Dairy products, antacids and iron do the same. Take doxycycline away from dairy and minerals.

nodes.q: If her acne stayed severe despite topical and oral antibiotic treatment, which oral drug would be used?
nodes.note: A vitamin A derivative that shrinks the oil glands and lowers sebum.

nodes.q: Which serious effect of isotretinoin depends on its binding to the retinoid X receptor (RXR)?
nodes.note: Fetal exposure causes craniofacial, heart and brain defects. Other effects: dry lips, raised triglycerides, liver enzyme rise, mood changes.

nodes.q: What must a woman have in place before starting isotretinoin?
nodes.a: A negative pregnancy test and reliable contraception, repeated monthly
nodes.note: In the US this is done through a registry program.

nodes.q: Her red facial papules and pustules could suggest rosacea. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Middle-aged adults. **Facial flushing, central face telangiectasias, papules and pustules but no comedones**

nodes.note: The trap: both give papules and pustules on the face, and both improve on tetracyclines.

nodes.q: Acne from excess androgens could suggest polycystic ovary syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: Her pustules could suggest folliculitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Uniform small pustules, each centered on a hair, without comedones**; from bacteria (often Staphylococcus aureus) or friction and shaving
**Mixed lesions: comedones, papules and pustules** on the face

nodes.q: Her red papules could suggest perioral dermatitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small papules around the mouth and nose that spare a thin rim next to the lips**, often after topical steroids; no comedones
**Comedones plus papules and pustules over the forehead, cheeks and nose**

nodes.q: Her hormone-driven skin changes could suggest precocious puberty. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Breast development before age 8 in a girl** (or testicular growth before 9 in a boy) with rapid growth
**Breast development starting at a normal age (here 11) with regular periods**; the androgen rise is normal timing

highlight: blistering sunburns after short periods outdoors
the skin under her clothes looks normal
hair and eye color are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A disorder of DNA repair. The clincher: **severe blistering sunburn after minimal sun exposure + early freckling and rough spots confined to sun-exposed skin in a toddler**.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern fits, given that her parents are first cousins?
nodes.note: Both parents carry one faulty copy of an XP gene; consanguinity raises the chance of two copies.

nodes.q: Which DNA repair pathway is defective?
nodes.note: Her cultured skin fibroblasts cannot repair ultraviolet damage. Base excision repair, mismatch repair and recombination repair are intact.

nodes.q: Which ultraviolet-induced DNA lesion stays in her skin cells?
nodes.note: Ultraviolet B light fuses adjacent pyrimidines, bending the helix. Normal cells cut out a short stretch of the damaged strand, then DNA polymerase and DNA ligase fill and seal the gap.

nodes.q: Which type of cancer is she at high risk of developing at a very young age?
nodes.a: Skin cancer (basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma)
nodes.note: The unrepaired dimers become mutations. Skin cancers can appear in childhood; the eyes and tongue tip are also affected.

nodes.q: Apart from the skin and eyes, which organ system is damaged in about a quarter of patients?
nodes.note: Neurons also accumulate unrepaired DNA damage and are lost early: progressive hearing loss, cognitive decline and ataxia (the most severe form is De Sanctis-Cacchione syndrome).

nodes.q: What is the cornerstone of management?
nodes.a: Strict lifelong avoidance of ultraviolet light, with sunscreen, protective clothing and regular skin and eye exams
nodes.note: No treatment fixes the repair defect. Remove skin cancers early.

nodes.q: Her blistering in the sun could suggest a porphyria. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sun blisters + red-brown urine + hemolytic anemia** and red-stained teeth; no freckling
**Dense freckling of exposed skin + normal urine and blood counts**

nodes.note: The trap: both give blisters after minimal sun exposure in early childhood.

nodes.q: Her sun sensitivity could suggest albinism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pale skin, hair and eyes from absent tyrosinase activity**, with nystagmus; burns but does not freckle
**Normal hair and eye color with dense freckling and mottled pigment in sun-exposed skin**

nodes.q: Her photosensitivity could suggest Cockayne syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Photosensitivity + growth failure, small head and premature aging, deafness**; defect in transcription-coupled repair, with no excess skin cancer
**Photosensitivity + freckling + normal growth**, with very high skin cancer risk

nodes.q: A DNA repair defect could also suggest ataxia telangiectasia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Unsteady gait + dilated small vessels of eyes and skin + recurrent sinus and lung infections**; defective repair of double-strand breaks (ATM gene)
**Steady gait + sun-induced freckling and blistering**; ultraviolet damage, not double-strand breaks

nodes.q: Her repair defect could be placed in base excision repair instead. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Removes a **single damaged base (for example uracil from cytosine deamination)** using a glycosylase; no striking ultraviolet sensitivity
Removes **bulky distorting lesions such as pyrimidine dimers**; causes severe sun sensitivity and skin cancer

root.stem: A 78-year-old man has had 1 week of itchy skin followed by large, tense blisters on his forearms, inner thighs and trunk. The blisters stay intact when touched, and rubbing normal-looking skin beside a blister does not make it slide off. He has no mouth sores. He has taken linagliptin for type 2 diabetes for 6 months. He has no fever, no target-shaped spots, no abdominal symptoms, and no history of blistering in childhood, and the blisters are not grouped on his elbows and knees. highlight: does not make it slide off
no history of blistering in childhood
not grouped on his elbows and knees
linear deposits of immunoglobulin G (IgG) and complement C3 along the dermal-epidermal junction

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An autoimmune blistering disease of older adults. The clincher: **tense blisters + no mouth sores + linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane**.

nodes.q: Which skin structure do the autoantibodies attack?
nodes.a: Hemidesmosomes (the BP180 and BP230 proteins) of basal keratinocytes
nodes.note: Pemphigoid targets cell-to-matrix attachments; pemphigus targets cell-to-cell attachments.

nodes.q: What does that structure normally do?
nodes.a: It attaches basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane (the extracellular matrix)
nodes.note: Losing it detaches the whole epidermis from the dermis, so the blister roof is thick and stays intact.

nodes.q: Which type of hypersensitivity is this?
nodes.note: IgG binds the hemidesmosome antigens and activates complement, which draws in eosinophils and neutrophils that damage the junction.

nodes.q: At which level of the skin does the blister form?
nodes.a: Subepidermal, between the epidermis and dermis
nodes.note: A full-thickness epidermal roof makes the blister tense and hard to rupture. The eosinophils on his biopsy are typical.

nodes.q: Which bedside sign was tested by rubbing the normal-looking skin beside a blister?
nodes.note: Absent in him: the epidermis stays attached to itself, so it does not slide off. It is present in pemphigus vulgaris, where keratinocytes separate from each other.

nodes.q: Which drug class, which he takes for diabetes, is a known trigger?
nodes.a: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors such as linagliptin
nodes.note: Loop diuretics such as furosemide and some other drugs can also trigger it.

nodes.q: Which treatment is first-line for localized or widespread disease?
nodes.note: Oral prednisone for extensive disease. Steroid-sparing options include doxycycline, methotrexate, mycophenolate and dupilumab (anti-interleukin-4 receptor alpha). Stop the suspected trigger drug.

nodes.q: His blisters could suggest pemphigus vulgaris. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Flaccid blisters that rupture into painful erosions, with mouth sores and a positive Nikolsky sign**; IgG against desmoglein 3 with a net-like pattern
**Tense intact blisters, no mouth sores, negative Nikolsky sign, linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane**

nodes.note: The trap: both are autoimmune IgG blistering diseases of older adults.

nodes.q: His itchy blisters could suggest dermatitis herpetiformis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Intensely itchy grouped vesicles on the elbows and knees, associated with celiac disease**; granular IgA at the dermal papillae tips
**Large tense blisters in a person without gluten symptoms and linear IgG and C3**

nodes.q: A drug could instead have caused a severe blistering reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, painful mucosal erosions and flat target-like spots that peel in sheets** days to weeks after a new drug; full-thickness epidermal necrosis
**Tense blisters on itchy skin over weeks, mouth spared, no fever, immune deposits at the basement membrane**

nodes.q: Blisters from weak skin attachment could suggest epidermolysis bullosa. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Blisters from minor trauma beginning in infancy or childhood**, genetic defect in keratin or anchoring proteins; no autoantibodies
**First blisters at age 78 without trauma, with linear IgG and C3 deposits**

palisading of the cells at the edge of each island

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common skin cancer. The clincher: **a pearly translucent nodule with fine blood vessels on sun-exposed skin + basophilic cell islands with edge palisading and clefts**. Larger lesions develop rolled edges and a central ulcer (rodent ulcer).

nodes.q: From which skin layer do the tumor cells arise?
nodes.a: The basal layer of the epidermis
nodes.note: It begins in the epidermis and grows downward through the basement membrane into the dermis. It does not start in the dermis, fat or fascia.

nodes.q: What explains the clear spaces around the tumor islands on the slide?
nodes.a: Retraction of the tumor from the surrounding stroma during tissue processing
nodes.note: Tumor cells line up at the edge of each nest (palisading) and shrink away from mucin-rich stroma.

nodes.q: Which environmental exposure is the main risk factor?
nodes.note: Cumulative and intermittent sun exposure in fair-skinned people damages DNA with pyrimidine dimers.

nodes.q: Which signaling pathway is overactive in most of these tumors?
nodes.note: Inherited PTCH1 mutation causes basal cell nevus (Gorlin) syndrome, with many tumors at a young age.

nodes.q: Which drug class blocks the pathway for advanced disease?
nodes.note: Used when surgery is not possible. Teratogenic.

nodes.q: How does the tumor typically behave?
nodes.a: Slow local invasion with very rare metastasis
nodes.note: It can destroy local tissue (nose, eyelid) but seldom spreads. Hence cure by complete removal is expected.

nodes.q: Which surgery gives the best cure rate for a facial tumor like his?
nodes.note: Layer-by-layer excision with immediate margin review spares tissue on the face.

nodes.q: His nodule could suggest squamous cell carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Scaly, crusted or ulcerated nodule, often arising from actinic keratosis; keratin pearls on biopsy**; classic on the lower lip; can metastasize
**Pearly translucent nodule with fine vessels; basaloid islands with palisading and clefts**; classic on the upper lip; rarely metastasizes

nodes.note: The trap: both occur on sun-exposed skin of older adults.

nodes.q: His lesion could suggest melanoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Asymmetric, irregular border, varied brown-black color, enlarging; atypical melanocytes** staining for S-100
**Symmetric pearly pink nodule without brown or black color; basophilic cell islands**

nodes.q: His lesion could suggest seborrheic keratosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Waxy, stuck-on, brown plaque with keratin-filled cysts (horn cysts) on biopsy**; benign
**Pearly nodule with surface vessels; invasive basophilic islands**

nodes.q: His sun-exposed skin could suggest actinic keratosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rough, sandpaper-like scaly patch with atypical keratinocytes in the lower epidermis**; precursor of squamous cell carcinoma
**Smooth pearly nodule; tumor islands extending through the basement membrane**

nodes.q: His nodule could suggest a melanocytic nevus (mole). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small uniform tan-brown macule or papule; nests of melanocytes at the dermal-epidermal junction (junctional) or also in the dermis (compound)**
**Pearly pink translucent nodule; basophilic tumor islands with clefts**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?

nodes.q: Which infection is the most common trigger overall?

nodes.q: Which hypersensitivity mechanism damages the skin?

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An overgrown scar. The clincher: **a firm scar that grows beyond the original wound edges, appearing weeks to months after the injury**.

nodes.q: Which process in wound healing is abnormal?
nodes.note: Fibroblasts keep making collagen long after the wound has closed, and the excess spreads past the wound edges with claw-like projections.

nodes.q: During normal scar remodeling, which collagen type replaces the early type III collagen?
nodes.note: Granulation tissue lays down type III collagen first; remodeling swaps it for stronger type I (a scar regains about 70-80% of normal strength by 3 months). In a keloid, fibroblasts overproduce both type I and type III collagen.

nodes.q: How does the collagen look on biopsy?
nodes.a: Thick, glassy (hyalinized), haphazardly arranged collagen bundles
nodes.note: A hypertrophic scar has collagen bundles running parallel to the skin surface.

nodes.q: Which growth factor drives the fibroblasts to overproduce collagen?
nodes.note: It stimulates fibroblast collagen and fibronectin synthesis and blocks matrix breakdown. Platelet-derived growth factor also recruits fibroblasts.

nodes.q: Which feature of her background most raises her risk?
nodes.note: Keloids are far more common in people with skin of color, peak at ages 10-30 and run in families (as in her mother).

nodes.q: Where is a keloid after piercing most classic?
nodes.note: Other common sites are the chest over the sternum, shoulders and upper back. Palms and soles are rarely affected.

nodes.q: What usually happens when a keloid is cut out with no other treatment?
nodes.a: It comes back, often larger than before
nodes.note: Recurrence after excision alone is common (in more than half), so excision is combined with steroid injection, pressure or radiation.

nodes.q: Which injected drug is first-line to shrink the scar?
nodes.note: Repeated injections every 4-6 weeks flatten and soften the scar. Silicone sheets, pressure and cryotherapy are other options.

nodes.q: How does the injected corticosteroid shrink the scar?
nodes.a: It suppresses fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis
nodes.note: It also reduces inflammation and increases collagen breakdown. Local side effects: skin thinning (atrophy), lighter skin and small dilated vessels.

nodes.q: Her thick scar could suggest a hypertrophic scar. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised scar that stays within the original wound margins**, appears within weeks, has parallel collagen bundles, often regresses and rarely recurs after excision
**Scar that grows beyond the wound margins**, appears weeks to months later, has disorganized collagen, rarely regresses and often recurs after excision

nodes.note: The trap: both are excess collagen scars that are firm, raised and itchy.

nodes.q: Her raised scar could suggest granulation tissue. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Soft, beefy red, moist and bleeding tissue in an open healing wound** with new capillaries and fibroblasts; temporary
**Firm, rubbery, shiny scar over closed skin, with dense collagen and little vascularity**
